text: BSCS agreed practice Feedback principles at BSCS At BSCS, effective feedback is underpinned by the following principles: At BSCS, effective feedback is underpinned by the following principles: Feedback begins with high-quality instruction. Clear explanations, modelling, guided practice and checks for understanding reduce the amount of feedback needed later. Feedback should not compensate for unclear teaching; it should build on strong lesson preparation, explicit instruction and responsive teaching. Feedback moves learning forward. Feedback should target specific learning gaps, misconceptions or next steps. The most effective feedback focuses on the task, the subject knowledge or the student’s self-regulation strategies, rather than vague praise or personal characteristics. Feedback is timely and proportionate. Feedback may be immediate, delayed, verbal, written, whole-class, peer-led or supported by technology. Teachers use professional judgement to choose the most appropriate method based on the task, the class and the learning need. Policies should not over-specify the frequency or method of feedback. Students must act on feedback. Feedback is only effective when students understand it and have time to use it. Teachers should plan opportunities for students to correct, redraft, rehearse, practise or extend their work so that the feedback loop is closed. Feedback should be manageable and sustainable. text: Individual Development CPD Developmental peer observation A short, focused protocol for observing one change and how pupils respond. Peer observation in Individual Development is developmental, not judgemental. The observer gathers focused evidence on one change and how pupils respond. text: Practitioner profile Cold calling Asking the question to the whole class, allowing thinking time and then warmly inviting a selected student to respond. What it is: Asking the question to the whole class, allowing thinking time and then warmly inviting a selected student to respond. Why it helps: Pause-then-name keeps every student accountable for thinking and produces a more representative sample than relying on volunteers. Participation ratio Participation ratio is the proportion of pupils actively engaged in the learning task at a given moment. Two variables matter: how many pupils are participating and for how long. Independent practice is a common point for the ratio to fall because pupils have more opportunity for a “cognitive break”. The aim is therefore sustained thinking, effort and accountability — not pupils merely looking busy. The project summary treated it as a tightly structured thinking and rehearsal routine: 1. Pose a question worth discussing. 2. Give individual thinking time first (at least a few seconds; often with a jot or MWB response). 3. Specify who speaks first using an unambiguous role. 4. Partner A explains while Partner B listens. 5. Switch so Partner B responds. 6. End while discussion is still lively — at the “crest of the wave”. 7. Harvest thinking through Cold Call, a re-vote, or a prompt that rewards listening rather than only speaking. Make sure there is something to discuss Turn and Talk is particularly productive when pupils have different answers, need to justify a method, or must compare reasoning. text: Adviser guidance How the BSCS adviser should answer 1. Role and boundaries The BSCS Evidence & Strategy Adviser is a direct-access teaching and learning consultant. It should help teachers understand what the strongest relevant evidence and BSCS professional knowledge suggest they should understand and do. It is intentionally distinct from the Strand 3 Enquiry Coach. Answer teaching-and-learning questions directly; do not default to the enquiry stages. Trust professional judgement. Evidence or baseline data may improve diagnosis, but are not prerequisites to receiving advice. Do not auto-generate a formal working hypothesis unless the teacher explicitly asks for diagnostic or enquiry support. Avoid prolonged questioning. If context is missing but useful advice is still possible, give the useful advice first. Use subject/phase context when supplied, but never assume a subject that the teacher has not stated. 2.
